# 05 · Concurrency: check many endpoints with a thread pool

*Sample output: what the model solution actually produces, on the input shown.*

## The main problem: health-checking a fleet without waiting for it

One endpoint at a time first, so the shape of a result is clear. Four outcomes, same
four keys every time, so a caller never needs a defensive `.get()`:

```python
# healthy
>>> check_endpoint('http://api.internal/health', timeout=2)
{'ok': True, 'status': 200, 'latency': '<0.00s>', 'error': None}

# up, but returning 500
>>> check_endpoint('http://checkout.internal/error', timeout=2)
{'ok': False, 'status': 500, 'latency': '<0.00s>', 'error': 'HTTP 500'}

# nothing listening
>>> check_endpoint('http://cache.internal/health', timeout=2)
{'ok': False, 'status': None, 'latency': '<0.00s>', 'error': 'ConnectionError: connection refused'}

# too slow, so we cut it off
>>> check_endpoint('http://reports.internal/slow', timeout=0.05)
{'ok': False, 'status': None, 'latency': '<0.00s>', 'error': 'ReadTimeout: read timed out'}
```
Reading that: `status` is `None` when there was no HTTP response at all, rather than 0,
because 0 would be a lie. A 500 is `ok: False` but still carries its status, which is the
difference between "the service is broken" and "the service is gone" — different pages,
different runbooks. The last case is the one that matters in production: without
`timeout=`, one blackholed host holds a worker thread until the process is restarted.

### Eight slow endpoints at once

```python
>>> results = check_endpoints([8 urls, each ~300ms], max_workers=8, timeout=2)
>>> len(results)
8
>>> all(r['ok'] for r in results.values())
True
```

Reading that: eight requests of roughly 300ms each finished in about the time of the
slowest one, not eight times that, because the pool had eight workers waiting on the
network in parallel. Drop `max_workers` to 1 and the same batch takes eight times as
long — the drill's tests assert exactly that difference. No measured number is printed
here, because it would change on every machine and every run.

### One dead host must not sink the batch

```python
>>> check_endpoints([api, checkout, cache], timeout=2)
http://api.internal/health             {'ok': True, 'status': 200, 'latency': '<0.00s>', 'error': None}
http://checkout.internal/error         {'ok': False, 'status': 500, 'latency': '<0.00s>', 'error': 'HTTP 500'}
http://cache.internal/health           {'ok': False, 'status': None, 'latency': '<0.00s>', 'error': 'ConnectionError: connection refused'}
```

Reading that: three results, one per URL, and the refused host did not stop the other
two from reporting. That is the whole reason `check_endpoint` returns errors instead of
raising them: `as_completed` hands back whatever finishes, in finish order, and the
dictionary comprehension maps each future back to the URL it came from.

## The variant: is the port even open?

```python
>>> check_ports([('db.internal', 5432), ('cache.internal', 6379)], timeout=1.0)
('cache.internal', 6379)         {'open': False, 'latency': '<0.00s>', 'error': 'ConnectionRefusedError: connection refused'}
('db.internal', 5432)            {'open': True, 'latency': '<0.00s>', 'error': None}

>>> summarize(results)
{'open': [('db.internal', 5432)], 'closed': [('cache.internal', 6379)]}
```

Reading that: this proves a TCP handshake completed, not that the service behind the
port is healthy — a database mid-crash-recovery accepts connections and answers nothing.
It is the right check for "is the firewall rule live?" and the wrong one for "can I
serve traffic?". Note also that `summarize` sorts, so the output is stable enough to
diff between runs, which is what makes it safe to feed to another tool.
